description: We're a team of curious minds interested in space, technology, and building things. Taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we aim to experiment, learn, and turn our ideas into something useful. Always open to new perspectives and people who love to create.
summary:
CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive mission-planning tool that helps evaluate potential lunar south-pole landing sites. It combines NASA datasets, including LOLA elevation maps, LROC imagery, and JPL SPICE ephemerides, to simulate the lunar environment at selected locations and times.

Users can explore 3D lunar terrain, visualize the Sun’s and Earth’s positions, identify terrain-obstructed sunlight and Earth visibility, and compare illumination periods and potential communication blackout windows across candidate sites.

The project addresses the challenge by turning complex orbital and terrain data into an accessible, interactive tool for understanding the conditions a lunar lander may experience. This is important because access to sunlight affects power generation, while Earth visibility is essential for communications. By bringing these factors together, the browser can help researchers and mission planners compare candidate locations and make better-informed decisions about future lunar missions.
details:
CLPS Lunar Mission Browser helps explore and compare potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole.

Users can view lunar terrain in 3D, select locations, and check how much sunlight and Earth visibility those locations get over time. We use NASA's LOLA terrain data and JPL SPICE to calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth while accounting for obstructions caused by nearby terrain. This helps identify periods of darkness and possible communication blackouts.

The goal is to make it easier to understand the conditions a lunar lander might face before choosing a landing site.

Tech stack: Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, React, TypeScript, and Three.js, using publicly available NASA and JPL datasets.

What makes the project different is that terrain isn't just visual. Hills, ridges, and crater walls directly affect the calculations. We also considered data accuracy, terrain resolution, performance, and the limitations of the available datasets.
